nipissing-community-account.creator: Nipissing First Nation, collective public community account
nipissing-community-account.peopleAndPlace: A particular Anishinaabe First Nation in Ontario; distinct from Richard Van Camp’s Tłı̨chǫ Nation and from every other First Nation.
nipissing-community-account.portion: Main introductory paragraph and first four programming bullets; not unrelated news, staff contacts or a claim that the old strategic-plan forecast is current.
nipissing-community-account.actualContentRead: The account identifies the Nation’s language priority and describes fluent speakers assisting learners, children’s language/culture programming and community communication.
nipissing-community-account.themeTask: Use actual details to explain a particular relationship among language, shared learning, generations and community agency. Identify what the text does and does not establish about earlier causes or every member’s experience.
nipissing-community-account.contextBoundary: The page describes revitalization and its own constitutional language priority. Do not infer that a particular person attended a residential school or that every past policy directly caused every described programme. A current programme description is not measured programme efficacy.

flett-lived-experience.creator: Julie Flett
flett-lived-experience.identity: Cree-Métis Canadian author, illustrator and artist
flett-lived-experience.portion: Actual 6September2019 interview: first answer’s walk/meeting/snowdrop gift; later answers about growing up among makers, Cree language in the story, creation process and intergenerational relationships. Adult prepares the selection and may omit grief passages; the complete interview body was read.
flett-lived-experience.actualContentRead: The creator relates a real neighbour connection and her artist/maker upbringing to the work, explains a language choice and describes how story, image and words developed.
flett-lived-experience.themeTask: Relate a supported creative choice to an attributed experience, compare the evidence with a different creator and distinguish the interview from the unread complete Birdsong book.
flett-lived-experience.contextBoundary: This is an actual interview text with its own first-person account. Do not invent a full book plot, imply that Cree and Métis identities are interchangeable, or call all Métis people mixed ancestry. The writer’s stated explanation supports particular influences; it is not a universal rule about Indigenous creativity.

audlaluk-memory-excerpt.creator: Larry Audlaluk
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.identity: Inuit memoir author with family roots in Nunavik and the experience of relocation to the High Arctic
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.portion: Publisher Spring2020 catalogue, printed/PDF page25, paragraphs1,2and4 only. Omit paragraph3’s unsafe sea-ice accident. Page24 supplies separate publisher context. The complete excerpt page was read and visually checked.
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.actualContentRead: The narrator distinguishes family stories about their earlier home from remembered scenes, connects later reflection with family/place and identifies roots in Nunavik.
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.themeTask: Explain a supported family, memory or place relationship; older pupils distinguish family-told information from a remembered scene and assess how relocation context can matter to this particular written account.
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.contextBoundary: The Spring catalogue is an identified prepublication excerpt, not proof of the exact final book text. No complete memoir or original government reports were read. The publisher supplies the early-1950s relocation context; the excerpt cannot establish every policy detail, every Inuit experience or a current 2026 biography claim. Do not simulate displacement, cold or danger.

van-camp-poetic-opening.portion: Actual short publisher-displayed poetic opening only, retaining Tłı̨chǫ creator attribution and illustrator credits.
van-camp-poetic-opening.task: Read an accessible selected portion, listen to the exact words read aloud and explain a supported relationship/care theme. No full book, picture sequence or national worldview is inferred.

ashevak-visual-work.portion: Actual complete museum-displayed1960 stonecut image, previously personally viewed, linked rather than redistributed.
ashevak-visual-work.task: View the actual arrangement and distinguish observable detail, own interpretation and an intention only the creator/source could establish. Preserve artist/printmaker/printer identities; do not present one work as all Inuit perspectives.

storywork-framework.frameworkAttribution: Jo-ann Archibald, Stó:lō scholar; a particular educational framework, not a universal claim about every Indigenous protocol.
storywork-framework.sourceCheck: The actual official glossary and creator’s educator-page main body were read; the linked videos were not watched and no transcript or closed traditional story is claimed.
taskPanel: Before sharing a selected publicly published life-experience text, name its actual creator, people/place and supplied context; respect the permitted portion and acknowledge that one voice is particular.

Prepare a receptive listening opportunity with accessible communication and optional reflection. Do not interrupt a narrator’s account to demand a single approved feeling or private learner disclosure.

Distinguish the narrator’s words from an own connection. Relate ideas, felt response, a chosen physical/visual response and a sense of connection or meaning without testing a pupil’s spiritual belief.

Return an attributed response or thoughtful question to the shared classroom discussion; do not extract a story into an anonymous universal moral. Compare how more than one perspective can contribute to meaning.
Explain a supported connection among person, family/community, place and another part of the account. Keep a fact, an inference and a question needing more evidence distinct.

For a traditional or restricted story outside this published portfolio, first establish the actual appropriate community/creator protocol; never invent permission or a culturally authentic substitute.
storywork-framework.limits: Original prepared classroom application informed by the named framework, not an author-validated implementation, ceremonial authority, moral-worth test or therapeutic/healing outcome.

principleTaskBindings.respect: Identify the actual people, creator and context; listen without replacing a particular voice with a generic group label.
principleTaskBindings.responsibility: Keep source words, own inference and unanswered questions distinct; check the permitted published portion and do not invent a traditional story.
principleTaskBindings.reciprocity: Offer an attributed response or thoughtful question to shared learning, acknowledging what the creator contributes rather than extracting an anonymous moral.
principleTaskBindings.reverence: Treat the shared account attentively and acknowledge its significance to its teller; no compulsory spiritual statement or emotional display.
principleTaskBindings.holism: Invite connections among ideas, an optional feeling, a chosen bodily/visual response and a sense of meaning without turning any belief or feeling into a score.
principleTaskBindings.interrelatedness: Support a real relation among person, family/community, place and another part of the account using actual evidence.
principleTaskBindings.synergy: Hear another supported reading and revisit an initial interpretation; explain how different contributions can deepen understanding without insisting everyone agrees.

themes-and-attribution.task: Use actual selected material from the First Nation community account, the Cree-Métis creator interview and the Inuit memoir, with the poetic/visual works as additional forms. Record creator, particular people/place, what the supplied portion actually communicates and a theme supported by a detail. Compare related care, language, family, making, place and memory ideas without assuming all creators share the same history or worldview. Preserve the distinction among First Nations, Métis and Inuit and the diversity within each.
themes-and-attribution.positive: The explanation names a particular source and a supporting detail rather than replaces meaning with a group label or a generic instruction to respect everyone.
themes-and-attribution.nearMiss: Every Indigenous person has one culture, a publisher biography is the actual story, or an invented universal theme is attributed to every community.
themes-and-attribution.transfer: Use a different actual portfolio text, explain a supported connection and identify an important difference or limit.

sourceDutyBindings.whoAndWhoseView: For every selected case, name the actual creator/collective and particular people/place. Distinguish narrator, publisher and reader viewpoints with actual evidence.
sourceDutyBindings.relationshipsAndContinuity: Use specific family, neighbour/maker or fluent-speaker/learner relationships and explain a supported connection between inherited experience and ongoing community/creative life.
sourceDutyBindings.knowledgeAndMeaning: Distinguish family-told knowledge, remembered/observed experience and the learner’s own inference; acknowledge the particular community account rather than invent a universal Indigenous truth.
sourceDutyBindings.identityAndAction: Explain how the particular text communicates belonging, making, language use, learning or community agency. Ground each idea in actual words or visible material, not a stereotype or a vocabulary recital.

read-listen-view-storywork.task: Across the portfolio actually read an appropriately supported selected written portion, listen to a creator’s exact published words read aloud, and view the actual attributed artwork. The manageable poetic excerpt and selected written lines provide actual pupil reading; an adult reads more demanding memoir/interview portions with stated context. Clarify unfamiliar place names rather than score prior familiarity. Discuss actual details, relationships and supported meaning. Grades4–6 enact the named storywork task panel while engaging with the published life-experience narratives; merely reciting seven principle names does not meet that requirement.
read-listen-view-storywork.positive: Reading, listening and viewing occur, and meaning is supported by actual words or visible evidence with source-specific attribution and the applicable framework practices.
read-listen-view-storywork.nearMiss: Listening to a synopsis replaces every actual reading duty, a whole book is claimed from an excerpt, or principle vocabulary alone replaces story engagement.
read-listen-view-storywork.transfer: Choose another identified portion or work and revisit an initial understanding after hearing another supported perspective.
read-listen-view-storywork.delivery: Adjust reading access and adult support honestly; if actual source access or a required modality is unavailable, retain that delivery condition rather than fabricate completed engagement.

context-and-present-connections.task: Build three separately attributed source cases. The Nation’s community text presents language priorities and shared transmission; Flett explicitly connects experience, maker relationships and a language choice to her creative work; Audlaluk’s excerpt connects family-told home/relocation memory and his own recalled scenes to a later written account. Separate creator statement, publisher context and own inference. Connect a supported continuity/change or present community/relationship issue using the actual sources, not an assumption that every contemporary person lives as in a past memoir. Grade-specific identification, explanation or assessment is in the panels. Carry out the explicit actualPresentConnection comparison and the three actualCaseChecks; the present relationship must be demonstrated with their stated evidence rather than left as a generic topic for discussion.
context-and-present-connections.positive: A concrete relation between an actual text and its supplied context is supported and bounded; a date alone or vague past-versus-now label is insufficient.
context-and-present-connections.nearMiss: All Indigenous texts are about the same trauma, every observed feature has an invented policy cause, or the narrator’s current life is inferred from a childhood scene.
context-and-present-connections.transfer: Evaluate a changed claim about a supplied text. Explain a supported link, a competing plausible reading where relevant and what additional evidence would be needed. No historical wrongdoing is justified simply because a practice existed.

wholeClaimBoundaries.identity: Current distinct-peoples identity claim remains unchanged; attribution does not mean a single creator speaks for everyone.
wholeClaimBoundaries.listening: The broader read-aloud topic retains its learner-relative beyond-independent-reading condition and wider narrative inventory.
wholeClaimBoundaries.history: The existing childhood-comparison claim retains its actual own-family interview requirement when assessed as a whole. A published memoir is not silently substituted as that completed interview.
wholeClaimBoundaries.meta: The older historical-context META card has bibliographic evidence strings; this proposal does not freshly certify that card as a validated assessment or use it to excuse harm. The explicit source-text tasks supply the current residual reasoning duty.

conditions: Use only the identified actual portions with appropriate adult preparation and access; metadata or invented authentic narratives are insufficient.
No curriculum or third-party work wording, lyrics, scores or images are copied into this report. Source links and original teaching designs are provided.
The four keyboarding-related positions have their separate actual task binding; other accepted historical Full judgments remain explicitly historical.

nipissing-community-account.question: What particular priority and shared-learning action does this Nation’s own account describe? How is a community’s transmission of language shown in actual details?
nipissing-community-account.expectedEvidence: The account states its own official-language priority and describes fluent speakers helping learners, children’s programming and community communication. These are particular source statements, not evidence of every person’s fluency or measured programme success.
nipissing-community-account.nearMiss: All First Nations use the same language, or a listed programme proves that every family attended and every historical harm was repaired.
nipissing-community-account.changedCase: If a different Nation has another language or programme, explain why this account cannot simply be relabelled as that Nation’s facts.

flett-lived-experience.question: Which actual experience and stated creative choice does this creator connect, and what is her own explanation rather than a reader’s guess?
flett-lived-experience.expectedEvidence: Flett describes repeated walks, meeting a neighbour, a snowdrop gift and maker relationships; she explains how connections, language and her creation process relate to the work. The interview provides those statements; it does not give the complete book for plot reconstruction.
flett-lived-experience.nearMiss: The interviewer’s question, the publisher’s biography and the creator’s own response are treated as the same voice, or every Cree and Métis person is assigned the neighbour’s experience.
flett-lived-experience.changedCase: Compare a claimed influence with the actual answer. Identify whether it is explicitly stated, reasonably inferred or unsupported by the supplied interview.

audlaluk-memory-excerpt.question: What information does the narrator say came through family storytelling, what scenes does he remember, and how does supplied relocation context help interpret the account?
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.expectedEvidence: The selected paragraphs connect the earlier home discussed by relatives, remembered family/place scenes and later reflection on roots. The separate publisher context identifies the early-1950s move. A child recollection and a family-told history are related sources of knowledge, not interchangeable records.
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.nearMiss: A childhood scene is called every Inuit person’s present life, or an unseen official report is claimed to have been compared with the memoir.
audlaluk-memory-excerpt.changedCase: A claim says the narrator personally witnessed every detail he heard from relatives. Use the distinction in the actual excerpt to explain what is supported and what remains uncertain.

actualPresentConnection.task: Compare the particular family/place transmission in Audlaluk’s selected account and the actual maker/intergenerational relationships Flett describes with the Nation’s present public account of shared language learning. Name one supported relation and one important difference. No learner family disclosure is needed.
actualPresentConnection.expectedEvidence: Each source shows a particular way knowledge or meaning can be shared through relationships. Audlaluk’s excerpt foregrounds a narrator’s family-told home memories and recalled scenes; Flett describes maker/neighbour relationships; the Nation’s public account describes organised language learning with fluent speakers and children’s programmes. Individual memoir, creator interview and collective programme account have different voices, places and purposes.
actualPresentConnection.limits: The comparison does not equate the peoples, prove that every current programme meeting occurred or infer every contemporary Inuit or Métis person’s life. The memoir alone cannot establish current community conditions.
actualPresentConnection.gradeUse: Grades1–3 identify a supported connection/difference; Grades4–5 explain it using details; Grade6 assesses the inference and identifies missing evidence for a stronger causal or universal claim.
